prompt.context: Your client is a supplier to manufacturers of biological drugs, also known as biologics. Biologics are manufactured through a complex process, and your client provides tanks, chemicals, steel pipes, and other inputs to that process. The biologics industry has been growing at a CAGR of 14% per year, and your client once shared similar growth. In the last few years, however, your client's growth has fallen to a CAGR of 4%.
prompt.question: What could be causing the slowdown in your client's revenue growth, and how can we fix it?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's primary objective?
clarifying_info.a: To increase revenues. We are not focusing on profitability.

clarifying_info.q: Are other suppliers experiencing the same slowdown?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Other suppliers to the biologics industry have been experiencing a similar slowdown in sales growth.

clarifying_info.q: How old is the client / how long has this industry existed?
clarifying_info.a: This is a new industry. Our client is only about a decade old, and our client's customers have been manufacturing biologics for a relatively short period of time.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been any changes in pricing?
clarifying_info.a: There has been no change in prices over the past few years.

clarifying_info.q: Has the volume of sales changed?
clarifying_info.a: Quantities have grown at a CAGR of 4% per year.
The product mix has remained relatively stagnant.

clarifying_info.q: Have new competitors entered the market?
clarifying_info.a: There have been no notable new entrants to the market.

clarifying_info.q: Have substitutes developed for the client's products?
clarifying_info.a: No substitutes have developed for the client's products.
Pharmaceutical companies (both major and minor) that produce biologics.

exhibits.title: Biologics Demand and Capacity
exhibits.shows: A line chart displaying historical data and projections (2008–2014e) for biologics demand and manufacturing capacity, both measured in millions of units. The two lines diverge over time, with demand rising above capacity in recent years and the gap widening through the forecast period.

data.y_axis: Millions of units, ranging from approximately 60 to 180
data.capacity_line: Rises initially then flattens, falling behind demand

framework: Revenue Economics: decompose revenue into Price x Quantity x Product Mix to isolate where growth has slowed
Price: check whether prices have been reduced
Quantity: check whether volume growth has stagnated
Product Mix: check whether the client is selling a higher proportion of lower-value items
Customers: assess customer segments (large, small, specialty), customer mix, and customer needs — key area for this case
Competitors: evaluate whether current competitors are scaling up, whether new entrants have arrived, and whether substitutes have emerged
Market: note that the overall market is growing at 14% CAGR, so the slowdown is client/supply-side, not market-wide

questions.prompt: After narrowing down that the problem is on the quantity (volume) side and ruling out price/mix/competition/substitutes, brainstorm: what could be causing customers to purchase fewer supplies?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify structural reasons tied to the capital-equipment nature of the products: (1) Tanks and pipes are long-lived assets — after an initial capacity ramp-up, customers do not need to replace them for many years; (2) Learning effects and experience curves allow customers to manufacture drugs more efficiently with less equipment over time; (3) Technological innovations have extended product lifespans (e.g., a tank that once lasted 2 weeks now lasts 2 months); (4) Biologics manufacturers have not been investing enough in new capacity to match growing demand — a key insight leading into Exhibit 1.

questions.prompt: Hand the candidate Exhibit 1. Our team has put together historical data and projections on demand and manufacturing capacity for biologics. What do you think?
questions.guidance: A good response identifies that after a brief period of overcapacity, demand is skyrocketing and leaving capacity far behind. A great response quantifies the shortage and proposes hypotheses for why it exists: (1) Does it take a long time to add capacity in this business? Yes. (2) Are manufacturers colluding to keep prices high? No. (3) Are there regulatory hurdles preventing new plants? No.

questions.prompt: What is the CAGR of the shortage between now (2011) and 2014?
questions.guidance: This question is designed to test comfort with numbers under pressure. Candidates should NOT try to use the exact CAGR formula — that takes too long. Approximation is the right approach. The key implication is that the shortage is growing at roughly 45% CAGR, far outpacing demand growth of 14%, which signals a massive capacity crunch ahead.

math.setup: Shortage in 2011 ≈ 20 million units; shortage in 2014e ≈ 60 million units. Find x such that 20 × (1+x)^3 = 60, i.e., (1+x)^3 = 3.
steps: Algebraic check: cube root of 3 is between 1.4 and 1.5, so x is between 40% and 50%, confirming ~45%
math.answer: ~45% CAGR for the shortage (vs. 14% CAGR for overall demand)

brainstorming.prompt: Assume we are fairly confident the numbers in Exhibit 1 are correct and demand will not pick up significantly through 2014. What are some other ways our client could increase revenues?

categories.name: Gain market share
ideas: Cut prices to undercut competitors and win more volume
Increase marketing spend and direct sales force to capture more orders
Innovate with better-quality products to justify premium pricing or displace rivals
Change product mix toward items that need to be replaced more frequently
Acquire a competitor to gain supplier power and potentially raise prices

categories.name: Create new revenue streams
ideas: Get into services to help biologics manufacturers meet the upcoming capacity shortage (e.g., engineering consulting, project management for plant expansion)
Begin selling additional inputs into the biologics manufacturing process beyond current product set
Enter the biologics manufacturing industry directly — massive market growth plus an acute capacity shortage make this an attractive option

recommendation: Our client should take advantage of the upcoming capacity shortage by pivoting into services that help biologics manufacturers ramp up their production capacity. This leverages the client's deep familiarity with the manufacturing process and addresses the single largest unmet need in the market through 2014 and beyond.
risks: Manufacturers may not be interested in ramping up capacity and may prefer to keep supply tight to drive up drug prices, reducing demand for the client's services
The client has no existing expertise in services, creating an execution and capability gap
The market for capacity-expansion services may already be saturated by engineering firms or other incumbents
next_steps: Speak directly with key customers (biologics manufacturers) to validate interest in and willingness to pay for capacity-expansion services
Assess the client's own internal capabilities and talent to determine what services it could credibly offer
Conduct a competitive assessment of the services market to understand saturation, pricing, and partnership opportunities
